$comment: The two rules `spec/format.md` §4.4 states with a ⛔ and nothing anywhere binds, because until
now no host read the value. Both are about what a reader does when the platform has moved on
and the installed plugin has not, which is the state every plugin spends most of its life in.
⛔ A value the host does not know reads as `tree`. The vocabulary is closed and the platform
owns it; it grows by GAINING values, and a new value is a new vocabulary version rather than a
change of meaning for an existing one. So the fallback is a named default, never a refusal and
never a guess: an unrecognised foliage type is a plant this reader has no family for, and a
tree is what the layer is otherwise made of.
⛔ A vocabulary id the host does not know is NO reason to ignore the column. This is the rule a
defensive reader gets backwards: seeing `"2"` where it was taught `"1"`, it drops the column
and reports a forest of trees, silently losing every shrub the platform DID publish in a value
it already understood. The values it knows keep their meaning and are mapped; only the ones it
does not fall back.
Values are matched EXACTLY. `Shrub` and `shrubland` are values this vocabulary does not contain,
so they take the same fallback -- a reader that case-folds or prefix-matches is inventing
members the platform never published, and the day `shrubland` means something else it is
already wrong.
⛔ The foliage type is NEVER derived from `height_m` or `crown_radius_m`. The rows below make a
reader that guesses fail: the shrub in the first row is TALLER than the tree beside it, because
the classification comes from the land-cover class under the point rather than from its size.
What this case does NOT bind: how a host LOGS any of it, and what it does when the manifest and
the header disagree about whether the column exists at all. §4.4 states neither, and a corpus
case that pinned one host's answer would oblige every other host to a decision it never made.
There is no `columns` list here. Every row's `csv` carries its own header, one row reorders it
and one omits the sixth column entirely, so a declared list would be a second statement of the
shape with nothing to check it against.
`csv` is the payload verbatim, newlines included. `foliageTypes` is one value per row the
reader produced, in order, in the vocabulary's own words. A reader that DROPS a row it cannot
classify fails on the count before it fails on a value: the foliage type is not one of the five
columns that make geometry, and losing a point over it is the layer thinning itself for a
reason no one can see.
Scoped to `revit` because it is the first host to read the column; Unreal's counterpart takes
the scope off. Nothing in the rules above is Revit's.

rows.name: the vocabulary this reader knows maps both its values, and neither from the dimensions
a value this reader does not know is a tree, and the values beside it are unharmed
a vocabulary this reader does not know still maps the values it does
the vocabulary's values are matched exactly, never by case and never by prefix
the column is found by header name, wherever the platform puts it
a manifest that names no vocabulary has no column to read: every point is a tree
